result.summary: Pindar says that Persephone sends back to the sunlight, in the ninth year, the souls of those from whom she accepts atonement for an ancient woe. These souls are reborn as kings and as strong, swift and wise men, who are later honored as holy heroes.

scenes.title: Persephone returns atoned souls
scenes.summary: Persephone accepts atonement for an ancient woe and sends souls back to the sun in the ninth year. They become kings and wise men, later called holy heroes.
scenes.stakes: Souls burdened by ancient guilt hope to be released from the underworld and win a return to life.

place.name: the world below and the light of the sun above

characters.name: Persephone
characters.description: queen of the dead who accepts atonement and sends souls back to the sun

notable_quotes.reason: Shows the belief that atoned souls are reborn as kings and heroes, honored as holy.

analysis.text: The fragment presents a hope of reincarnation and reward after death. Atonement for old guilt leads to rebirth in noble and heroic lives.

It reflects Orphic and Pythagorean-influenced ideas of soul-cycles and purification, which differ from the usual Homeric picture of a joyless afterlife. Such beliefs were found in southern Italy and Sicily, where Pindar had patrons.

fun_facts.text: The fragment is quoted by Plato in the Meno to support the idea that the soul is immortal and is born again.

language_notes.text: "From whomsoever" is archaic: it means "from those people from whom" Persephone accepts the payment. The "atonement" is made by the souls, or on their behalf, to her.
"An ancient woe" is unexplained. It probably refers to an old guilt or ancestral wrong requiring compensation, a belief tied to Orphic and Pythagorean ideas of rebirth.
"Through the after-time" means in all later ages; the people of the future will call them holy heroes.

context_notes.text: Persephone is queen of the underworld, wife of Hades. Here she judges the dead and grants some of them a return to the upper world.
Heroes in Greek belief were exalted figures of the past who received cult honours after death, standing between mortals and gods.

literary_notes.text: "The light of the sun above" stands for life in the upper world, set against the darkness of the underworld.
The series "swift and strong and in wisdom very great" piles up praising attributes, defining the ideal of the noble man in Pindar's world.
